title: Two pockets
hook: Rabbi Simcha Bunim: one note says "for my sake the world was made", the other "I am dust and ashes"

segments.voice: Yesterday Reb Zusya feared being asked why he wasn't Zusya. Your line was be Zusya. Did you do one thing that's truly yours? Day two hundred ninety-nine.

Some days you feel like you're nothing. You made a mistake at work, or said the wrong thing, and the voice in your head says you don't matter at all. Other days you feel like the center of the universe, and the voice says everyone should notice. Most of us swing between those two, sometimes in the same afternoon. A Hasidic rebbe in Poland had a remedy for this. It fits in your clothes. All you need is two pockets, and two slips of paper.
screen: `SOME DAYS: I'M NOTHING.` → `OTHER DAYS: I'M EVERYTHING.` → `TWO POCKETS, TWO SLIPS.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa lived around 1800. He's remembered as a sharp, honest teacher who hated pretending. The teaching attributed to him goes like this: every person should have two pockets. In one pocket, a note that says: for my sake the world was created. In the other: I am dust and ashes. And the wisdom is knowing which pocket to reach into, and when. Both lines are old. The first comes from the Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin. It teaches that God created the first human being alone, to show that each single life is a whole world. So every person is obligated to say: for my sake the world was created. The second comes from Genesis. Abraham, bargaining with God to save the city of Sodom, stops himself and says he is "but dust and ashes." Here's the trick. When you're low, when you feel worthless, reach into the first pocket. The world was made for you; your life is a whole world. When you're puffed up, sure you're owed, reach into the second: you're dust and ashes, and so is everyone else. Neither note alone is the truth. A person who only carries the first becomes arrogant. A person who only carries the second is crushed. Together, they hold you in the middle, which is where Abraham stood: humble, and bold enough to argue with God.
screen: `TWO POCKETS, TWO NOTES.` · `FOR MY SAKE THE WORLD WAS MADE.` · `I AM BUT DUST AND ASHES.` · `REACH FOR THE ONE YOU NEED.` · then, large: `TWO POCKETS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fill your pockets. Settle, and breathe. Put one hand on your right pocket, or your right side. Think: for my sake the world was made. Let it land. Your life is a whole world. Now put the other hand on your left side. Think: I am dust and ashes. Let that land too, gently. Feel both at once. Neither one crushes you or lifts you too high. You might even write them on two slips of paper and carry them today. The bell holds the time.
Two pockets. One note says for my sake the world was made. The other says I am dust and ashes. Reach for the one you need.
Your line: two pockets. Today, when you feel small, reach for the first note; when you feel too big, reach for the second. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Many Jews know Rabbi Simcha Bunim's two-pockets teaching, and some literally carry the two sayings on slips of paper as a reminder of balance between dignity and humility.

what it means: dignity and humility, carried together, each for its moment.
what a scholar hears: it joins Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 with Genesis 18:27, and is attributed to Simcha Bunim of Peshischa in later Hasidic collections.

sources.ref: Hasidic teaching attributed to Simcha Bunim of Peshischa

notes: Simcha Bunim of Peshischa (Przysucha), c. 1765–1827. The two-pockets saying is attributed to him in later collections (notably Buber's, copyrighted); paraphrased.
Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 paraphrased ('therefore each person must say: for my sake the world was created').
Genesis 18:27 JPS 1917: 'who am but dust and ashes'; please confirm.
The index hook uses quotation marks for the two notes; kept as in the index.
